Week 5 \| Fall 2026]{.custom-subtitle} ::: ::::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Goals for today (and next time) :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width='50%'} ::: {.nonincremental .fragment} **Today:** - Discuss the bootstrap for conducting inference - Implement bootstrapping in R ::: ::: ::: {.column width='50%'} ::: {.nonincremental .fragment} **Next time:** - Model and feature selection criteria ::: ::: :::: # First: choosing folds (Week 4, Wednesday slides) # The Bootstrap ## Another resampling method CV may remind you of another **resampling**: the Bootstrap! ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} There are differences in methodology and purpose: + CV: Model selection, model assessment, predictive accuracy + Bootstrap: Conducting inference within a given model In short: The bootstrap is a super general tool for **approximating sampling distributions**. ::: ## Discussion: Sampling Distributions Suppose we have the following linear regression model: $$ \hat{Y} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X_1 + \hat \beta_2 X_2 + \hat \beta_3 X_1X_2 $$ We would like to conduct inference (e.g., confidence intervals and hypothesis tests) on the parameter $\beta_3$ using the statistic $\hat\beta_3$ ::: {.nonincremental} 1. The statistic $\hat\beta_3$ has a sampling distribution. What is a sampling distribution, in your own words? 2. Why can't we directly construct the sampling distribution for $\hat\beta_3$? 3. In regression, under what conditions can we still conduct theory-based (i.e., sampling distribution-based) inference? ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
01:30
``` ::: ::: ## Sampling and Bootstrap Distributions Recall the **Samping Distribution** of a **Statistic** ($\hat{\theta}$), calculated from a **Sample** of size $n$ ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - Hypothetically, suppose we drew many random samples of size $n$ from the **population** - In each sample, we computed the statistic of interest, $\hat{\theta}$ ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - **The distribution of those statistics is the sampling distribution** - **Standard Error:** the standard deviation of the sampling distribution ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - **The Problem:** We can't draw multiple random samples of size $n$! - Under certain conditions, we can approximate sampling distributions using statistical theory. ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-up .midi .center} **Solution**: the bootstrap! ::: ## The Bootstrap ::: {.nonincremental} **The Bootstrap:** - We can *always* draw a **bootstrap sample** of size $n$ by sampling *with replacement* from your original sample $n$ times (i.e., equal to the original sample size) ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - Draw many bootstrap samples, and compute the **statistic of interest** in each - The distribution of *those* statistics makes up the **Bootstrap Distribution** - Bootstrap distributions can often well-approximate the **variability** of the sampling distribution. ::: ## Example Let's simulate a sample of data ($n=100$) from: $$Y = 1+ 2\cdot X_1 + 3\cdot X_2 + X_1 X_2 + \epsilon \ \ \ \text{where} \ \ \ \epsilon \sim N(0, \text{sd} = 0.5)$$ ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center" output-location='column-fragment'} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="1-7|9-14"} set.seed(10101) n <- 100 X1 <- runif(n, 0, 1) X2 <- runif(n, 0, 1) e <- rnorm(n, 0 ,.5) Y <- 1 + 2*X1 + 3*X2 + X1*X2 + e d <- data.frame(X1, X2, Y) ggplot(d, aes(x = X1, y = Y, color = X2)) + geom_point() + theme_bw() + labs(title = "One Sample from True Model") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk05mon_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ::: ## Model fit to the sample ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} my_mod <- lm(Y ~ X1*X2, data = d) summary(my_mod)$coefficients ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 1.447174 0.2100171 6.890742 5.807042e-10 X1 1.317290 0.3803365 3.463485 7.982768e-04 X2 2.405724 0.4102938 5.863417 6.404175e-08 X1:X2 2.044325 0.7415455 2.756844 6.985948e-03 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} b3 <- my_mod$coefficients["X1:X2"] b3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` X1:X2 2.044325 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - **Reminder:** The true $\beta_3 = 1$ We will compare the Sampling Distribution and Bootstrap Distribution ::: ## Sampling Distribution To construct the sampling distribution, I generate data from the *true model* many times. Each time, I fit a regression model to the data and save $\hat\beta_3$. NOTE: In the real world, **we can't do this** because we never know the true model! ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="1-6|8-17"} set.seed(234) trials <- 2000 # Number of random samples n <- 100 # Size of each random sample X1 <- runif(n, 0, 1) # Generate X1 (the same for all sims) X2 <- runif(n, 0, 1) # Generate X2 (the same for all sims) slopes<-data.frame() #Create empty dataframe for the beta3's for (i in 1:trials){ sim_e <- rnorm(n, 0 ,.5) # Simulate Error sim_Y <- 1 + 2*X1 + 3*X2 + X1*X2 + sim_e # Simulate Y sim_d <- data.frame(X1, X2, sim_Y) # Combine into dataframe sim_mod <- lm(sim_Y ~ X1*X2, data = sim_d) # Run model slopes <- rbind( slopes, data.frame(slope = sim_mod$coefficients["X1:X2"]) ) } ``` ::: ::: ## Sampling Distribution ::: {.cell layout-align="center" output-location='column-fragment'} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(slopes, aes(x = slope)) + geom_histogram(bins = 25, color = "white") + theme_bw() + labs(title = "Simulated Distribution of Slopes")+ geom_vline(xintercept = 1, color = "red", size = 1) + annotate(geom = "text", x = 0, y = 200, size = 8, label = "True Slope", color = "red") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk05mon_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} slopes %>% summarize(mean_slope = mean(slope), sd_slope = sd(slope)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mean_slope sd_slope 1 0.9885715 0.6731534 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## One Bootstrap Sample We have 1 sample: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} str(d) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 'data.frame': 100 obs. of 3 variables: $ X1: num 0.19 0.911 0.228 0.825 0.916 ... $ X2: num 0.106 0.675 0.175 0.736 0.843 ... $ Y : num 1.28 4.69 2.46 5.72 6.85 ... ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} But we can create a bootstrap sample: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="1-3|2|3"} set.seed(135) boot_indx <- sample(x = 1:n, size = n, replace = TRUE) a_bootstrap_sample <- d[boot_indx, ] str(a_bootstrap_sample) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 'data.frame': 100 obs. of 3 variables: $ X1: num 0.19 0.505 0.976 0.438 0.202 ... $ X2: num 0.106 0.749 0.603 0.177 0.581 ... $ Y : num 1.28 4.59 4.76 2.72 3.44 ... ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} How many observations from the original sample show up (at least once)? ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} length(unique(boot_indx)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 66 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Multiple Bootstrap Samples Can use the `rsample` package from `tidymodels` to create bootstrap samples ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(rsample) bt_resamples <- bootstraps(d, times = 1000) # 1000 samples ``` ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} The `bootstraps` function (much like the `vfold_cv` function) stores results as a `resample` object with 2 parts: - **`id`**, a vector with bootstrap sample identifiers (i.e "Bootstrap0001", "Bootstrap0002", ... ) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} length(bt_resamples$id) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1000 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} bt_resamples$id[1:5] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Bootstrap0001" "Bootstrap0002" "Bootstrap0003" "Bootstrap0004" [5] "Bootstrap0005" ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - **`splits`**, an `R` list that stores the indices of the original data for the bootstrap samples ::: ## Multiple Bootstrap Samples Can look at the individual bootstrap samples by Comparison of mean and sd for the bootstrap and sampling distributions: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 5 method mean_slope sd_slope q.025 q.975 1 bootstrap 1.99 0.714 0.504 3.38 2 sampling 0.989 0.673 -0.320 2.30 ``` ::: ::: ## How do we use this bootstrap distribution? **Confidence Intervals:** for a $C$-level interval, :::: {.columns} ::: {.fragment .nonincremental .column} - **Standard Error Method:** Calculate the bootstrap standard error (SE). Then the interval is: $$ \text{Statistic} \pm z^{*}_{C} * \text{SE} $$ where $z^{*}_{C}$ is the $(\frac{1+C}{2})$th quantile of a standard normal distribution ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} Bootstrap_SE <- sd(boot_slope$estimate) Statistic <- mean(boot_slope$estimate) zstar_95 <- qnorm((1+.95)/2, mean = 0, sd = 1) c( Statistic - zstar_95*Bootstrap_SE, Statistic + zstar_95*Bootstrap_SE ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.5863416 3.3847871 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental .column} - **Percentile Method:** use the $(\frac{1-C}{2})$th quantile of the bootstrap distribution for the lower bound, and the $(\frac{1+C}{2})$th quantile for the upper bound. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} c( quantile(boot_slope$estimate, (1 - .95) / 2), quantile(boot_slope$estimate, (1 + .95) / 2) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2.5% 97.5% 0.5035653 3.3795478 ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## How do we use this bootstrap distribution? ::: {.small} **Hypothesis Tests:** For a statistic, $\hat{\theta}$, that estimates the parameter, $\theta$, we can test: $$ H_0: \theta = \theta_0 \qquad \qquad H_A: \theta \neq \theta_0 \ \ \ \text{or} \ \ \ \theta < \theta_0 \ \ \ \text{or} \ \ \ \theta > \theta_0 $$ by calculating the test statistic: $$ T = \frac{\hat{\theta} - \theta_0}{\text{SE}} $$ and calculating the appropriate p-value based on a standard normal distribution. ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **Example**: $$H_0: \theta = 1 \quad \text{ vs. } \quad H_A: \theta\neq 1$$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} Bootstrap_SE <- sd(boot_slope$estimate) # Bootstrap_SE Statistic <- mean(boot_slope$estimate) # theta_hat Tstatistic <- (Statistic - 1) / Bootstrap_SE # T 2 * (1 - pnorm(Tstatistic, mean = 0, sd = 1)) # two-sided p-value ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.1674232 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Bootstrapping Other Statistics So far in 141 and 243, we've bootstrapped regression coefficients and other nice statistics (e.g., sample means). ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} But bootstrapping works for assessing uncertainty in tons of situations! + Joint uncertainty of multiple coefficients at once + $R^2$ value of a model + Predictions made using a model + etc. ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} The procedure is always the same: 1. Draw many bootstrap samples. 2. Compute the statistic of interest in each 3. Use the bootstrap distribution to approximate the variance of the statistic and thus conduct inference. ::: ## Pros and Cons of the Bootstrap ::: {.nonincremental} **Pro:** **When data is drawn randomly and independently from the population, bootstrap usually works for inference** - Thus, we don't always need to derive theoretical sampling distributions! ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - Also nice: **in linear regression, bootstrap inference works with only Linearity and Independence!** (i.e., don't need Normality or Equal Variance) ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - Bootstrap works for almost any kind of statistic! $R^2$, coefficients, sample means, predictions at a test point, etc. ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **Con:** Computationally intensive - May not be realistic with very complicated analyses or models (e.g., Neural Networks) ::: ## CV versus Bootstrapping Both are computationally intensive methods that involve sampling from your data set to learn more about your estimate/model. :::: {.columns} ::: {.fragment .nonincremental .column} **Cross-validation**: Often used to assess ***predictive accuracy*** (for model assessment and model selection purposes) - Partition data into folds - Fit model to training folds, predict on test fold - Iterate though all possible *folds* - Compute aggregate measure of predictive ability ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental .column} **Bootstrapping**: Often used for ***inference*** - Draw a bootstrap sample of size $n$ from your data *with replacement*. - Compute estimate of interest - Do this many times, obtaining many bootstrap estimates over many bootstrap samples - Consider distribution of bootstrap estimates ::: :::: ## Next time: ::: {.nonincremental} - Model selection and feature selection :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
